title: Divisibility Rules OQ-01-OQ-02-OQ-01: Exactly Which Moduli Admit a Power-of-10 Alternating-Digit-Sum Rule
description: Resolves the first open question of the parent (divisibility-rules-oq-01-oq-02): for which moduli d coprime to 10 does a power-of-10 alternating-digit-sum divisibility rule exist? A base 10^k alternating rule holds exactly when 10^k ≡ -1 (mod d), so the question is whether -1 is a power of 10 in ZMod d. The answer is a clean cyclic-group criterion proved here: for d ≥ 3 coprime to 10, such a base exists iff ord_d(10) is even and 10^{ord_d(10)/2} ≡ -1 (mod d), and then the minimal working base is 10^{ord_d(10)/2}. The mathematical core is a general monoid fact (involution_mem_powers_iff): an involution x ≠ 1 is a power of g iff orderOf g is even and g^{orderOf g/2} = x. Connected to the concrete divisibility test via an inlined alternating-digit-sum workhorse, this yields genuine new alternating rules (base 10^3 for 7 and 13) and explains the non-existence for 3 and 9 (where 10 ≡ 1). Fully machine-checked, 0 sorries, no axioms beyond Lean's foundational triple; all finite checks use kernel `decide` (not native_decide), so the file is free of Lean.ofReduceBool.

Main result neg_one_isPow_ten_iff: for d ≥ 3 coprime to 10, -1 is a power of 10 in ZMod d iff ord_d(10) is even and 10^{ord_d(10)/2} ≡ -1 (mod d) — the exact criterion for a power-of-10 alternating-digit-sum base to exist

overview.historicalContext: The divisibility-by-11 rule — a number is divisible by 11 iff its alternating digit sum is — works because 10 ≡ -1 (mod 11). More generally a base B alternating-digit-sum rule for d holds exactly when B ≡ -1 (mod d). The parent entry divisibility-rules-oq-01-oq-02 proved that the ordinary (non-alternating) digit-sum rule is universal: a power-of-10 base exists for every d coprime to 10, because some power of 10 is ≡ 1 (mod d) (Fermat–Euler). It explicitly flagged the alternating analogue as open and noted that, unlike the plain digit-sum rule, it is NOT universal — it fails for 3 and 9. This entry settles that open question with the exact existence criterion, which is the classical fact that a cyclic group of even order has a unique element of order two, namely g^{order/2}.
overview.problemStatement: Characterize exactly which moduli d coprime to 10 admit a power-of-10 alternating-digit-sum divisibility rule. Equivalently (since a base 10^k alternating rule holds iff 10^k ≡ -1 (mod d)): for which d is -1 a power of 10 in ZMod d? Show the criterion is that ord_d(10) is even and 10^{ord_d(10)/2} ≡ -1 (mod d), and identify the minimal working base.
overview.proofStrategy: The heart is a general monoid lemma involution_mem_powers_iff. Forward: from g^k = x with x^2 = 1, x ≠ 1, one gets orderOf g ∣ 2k but orderOf g ∤ k; an odd order would be coprime to 2 and force orderOf g ∣ k, so orderOf g is even; writing the order as 2h, h ∣ k with the quotient odd, and since g^h is an involution, g^k = (g^h)^{odd} = g^h = x, pinning the exponent to orderOf g/2. Backward is immediate. Specializing g = (10 : ZMod d), x = -1 (an involution distinct from 1 once d ≥ 3, since otherwise 2 = 0 i.e. d ∣ 2) gives neg_one_isPow_ten_iff via the parent's orderOf_ten_pos. The bridge pow_ten_zmod_eq_neg_one_iff rewrites (10 : ZMod d)^k = -1 as 10^k % d = d - 1 (using ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff and that d-1 casts to -1), feeding an inlined alternating-digit-sum workhorse (modEq_alternating_digits_sum: when b ≡ -1 (mod d), n ≡ alternating base-b digit sum) to produce a genuine divisibility test.
keyInsights: A base B alternating-digit-sum rule for d is exactly the congruence B ≡ -1 (mod d); for B = 10^k this is (10 : ZMod d)^k = -1, i.e. -1 must lie in the cyclic group generated by 10.
Whether -1 is a power of g is a pure cyclic-group question: -1 is an involution, and a cyclic group of even order 2h has a unique order-two element g^h, while a cyclic group of odd order has none.

Hence the criterion is precisely 'ord_d(10) even and 10^{ord_d(10)/2} ≡ -1', and when it holds the minimal working exponent is ord_d(10)/2 (strictly smaller than the full order used by the plain digit-sum rule).
Coprimality of 10 and d makes 10 a unit of finite order; the extra threshold d ≥ 3 is exactly what makes -1 ≠ 1, so that -1 is a genuine involution to locate.

This explains the classics: ord_11(10) = 2 gives the base-10 rule for 11; ord_7(10) = ord_13(10) = 6 give NEW base-10^3 alternating rules for 7 and 13; ord_3(10) = ord_9(10) = 1 is odd, so 3 and 9 admit no alternating rule.
Using kernel `decide` for the finite ZMod checks keeps the entry free of Lean.ofReduceBool — genuinely 0-axiom.
prerequisites: Multiplicative order in a monoid (orderOf, orderOf_dvd_iff_pow_eq_one, orderOf_dvd_of_pow_eq_one)
Elementary parity / coprimality of ℕ (Nat.coprime_two_right, Even/Odd, mul_dvd_mul_iff_left)
Modular arithmetic: Nat.ModEq, Int.ModEq (Int.modEq_iff_dvd), and ZMod d casts (ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff, ZMod.natCast_self)
Nat.digits / Nat.ofDigits and the alternating-digit-sum congruence (inlined here from the oq-01 parent)
The parent divisibility-rules-oq-01-oq-02 for orderOf_ten_pos (positivity of ord_d(10) for coprime d)

conclusion.summary: Ten theorems (two definitions) settle exactly which moduli admit a power-of-10 alternating-digit-sum rule. The general lemma involution_mem_powers_iff shows an involution x ≠ 1 is a power of g iff orderOf g is even and g^{orderOf g/2} = x; specialized to 10 and -1 in ZMod d (d ≥ 3 coprime to 10) it gives the criterion ord_d(10) even and 10^{ord_d(10)/2} ≡ -1, with minimal base 10^{ord_d(10)/2}. A bridge to the concrete alternating-digit-sum test yields new base-10^3 rules for 7 and 13 and confirms non-existence for 3 and 9.
conclusion.implications: Together with the parent (which settled the non-alternating digit-sum rule universally), this completes the existence theory for power-of-10 digit-sum-style rules: the plain rule exists for every coprime d, while the alternating rule exists iff the extra even-order/half-power criterion holds. The proof isolates the phenomenon as the classical uniqueness of an order-two element in a cyclic group, and remains 0-axiom and native_decide-free.
openQuestions: Radix-r generalization: for an arbitrary base r coprime to d, an alternating-digit-sum rule in base r^k exists iff -1 is a power of r in ZMod d, i.e. ord_d(r) is even and r^{ord_d(r)/2} ≡ -1 (mod d); involution_mem_powers_iff already proves the group-theoretic core for any g.
Combine the plain and alternating criteria to characterize the full set of 'block' rules (period-2k grouping with signs ±1) available for a given modulus, and the minimal block length for each.

sections.title: Part 0: Alternating-Digit-Sum Workhorse (inlined)
sections.summary: Self-contained re-derivation (from the oq-01 parent) of the alternating digit sum and its key congruence: alternatingDigitSum, altDigitSum, alternatingDigitSum_cons, ofDigits_modEq_alternatingDigitSum, and modEq_alternating_digits_sum — when the base b ≡ -1 (mod d), a number is congruent to its alternating base-b digit sum. Inlined so the file does not depend on the parent's build.

sections.title: Part I: The Cyclic-Group Characterization
sections.summary: involution_mem_powers_iff: in any monoid, an involution x (x^2 = 1) distinct from 1 lies in the cyclic group generated by g iff orderOf g is even and g^{orderOf g/2} = x. The forward direction derives orderOf g ∣ 2k but ∤ k, forces even order, and pins the witness exponent via a parity argument with the involution g^{orderOf g/2}.

sections.title: Part II: Specialization to 10 and -1 in ZMod d
sections.summary: neg_one_ne_one_zmod (d ≥ 3 makes -1 ≠ 1 since otherwise d ∣ 2), the main criterion neg_one_isPow_ten_iff (for d ≥ 3 coprime to 10, -1 is a power of 10 iff ord_d(10) is even and 10^{ord_d(10)/2} = -1), and minimality exists_pos_pow_ten_eq_neg_one (the minimal positive witness is ord_d(10)/2).

sections.title: Part III: Bridge to the Concrete Modular Condition
sections.summary: cast_pred_eq_neg_one (d-1 casts to -1 in ZMod d) and pow_ten_zmod_eq_neg_one_iff: the ZMod condition (10 : ZMod d)^k = -1 is exactly the concrete statement 10^k % d = d - 1 that drives the alternating rule.

sections.title: Part IV: The Alternating-Digit-Sum Divisibility Test
sections.summary: alt_rule_of_pow_eq_neg_one: whenever (10 : ZMod d)^k = -1, the base 10^k validates a genuine alternating-digit-sum divisibility test d ∣ n ↔ d ∣ (alternating base-10^k digit sum), via the inlined workhorse.

sections.title: Part V: Concrete Instances
sections.summary: Kernel-decide examples: base 10^1 for 11 (10 ≡ -1), NEW base 10^3 for 7 and 13 (10^3 ≡ -1), and non-existence for 3 and 9 (10 ≡ 1, so every power of 10 is 1 ≠ -1). #check commands expose the headline theorem names.
